name: application/vnd.mermaid
description:
Mermaid diagrams are written as plain text and rendered to SVG. A flowchart or sequence diagram is therefore stored in version control and reviewed as a diff, rather than as an opaque attachment that has to be opened.

The syntax is line-oriented: name the diagram type, then declare nodes and the edges between them. Built-in rendering in GitHub and GitLab markdown is why it spread beyond its own tooling.

name: application/vnd.apache.parquet
description:
Parquet is the Apache Software Foundation's columnar storage format. Values from a single column are stored together. A query touching three columns out of two hundred therefore reads only those three, and each column compresses well because everything in it is alike.

A file also carries its own schema and per-column statistics, letting a reader skip entire row groups that cannot satisfy a predicate. That combination is why it became the default for analytical data at rest. Where Parquet optimises storage, [application/vnd.apache.arrow.file](/application/vnd.apache.arrow.file) optimises passing data between processes.

name: application/vnd.apache.arrow.file
description:
Arrow's IPC (inter-process communication) file format writes a columnar table to disk. A footer holds the schema and the position of every record batch, so a reader can seek directly to any batch instead of scanning from the start.

The point is Arrow's in-memory layout. Because the file holds the same representation the library already uses in memory, reading is closer to mapping than to parsing. The form without a footer, for pipes and sockets, is [application/vnd.apache.arrow.stream](/application/vnd.apache.arrow.stream).

name: application/vnd.apache.arrow.stream
description:
This is the streaming form of Arrow's IPC (inter-process communication) format. It is a schema message followed by record batches, written and read strictly in order, with no footer at the end.

Having no footer means there is nothing to seek to, so a consumer cannot jump to the tenth batch. It also means the stream does not have to exist in full before reading starts. That is what makes this the right choice over a socket or a pipe, where the random access of [application/vnd.apache.arrow.file](/application/vnd.apache.arrow.file) was never available anyway.

name: text/vcard
description:
vCard is the contact format defined by RFC 6350, which specifies version 4.0. A card is a run of properties such as `FN`, `TEL`, `EMAIL` and `ADR`, between `BEGIN:VCARD` and `END:VCARD` lines. One file may hold many cards in sequence.

It is what an address book exports and what a phone attaches when someone shares a contact. The registration lists both extensions, but `.vcf` is the one almost every implementation writes.

name: text/xml
description:
RFC 7303 registers `text/xml` alongside `application/xml` for XML documents. The two are functionally equivalent, and the RFC recommends [application/xml](/application/xml) for general use.

The distinction is historical. A `text/` type once implied the content was readable without special tooling. The two types also differed in how a missing charset parameter was interpreted. RFC 7303 settled that: both now default the same way, leaving little reason to prefer this spelling beyond the many servers already sending it.

name: application/vnd.api+json
description:
JSON:API is a convention for building JSON APIs. It fixes how resources, relationships, pagination, filtering, sparse field selection and errors are shaped, so those decisions stop being renegotiated on every project.

The media type is part of the specification rather than incidental to it. A server signals JSON:API semantics by sending this type, and a client asks for them by content negotiation on it. That is why the type matters more here than for most JSON formats.

name: text/x-opml
description:
OPML (Outline Processor Markup Language) is an XML format for nested outlines. Its dominant use by a wide margin is exchanging feed subscription lists. Nearly every feed reader imports and exports OPML, which is what makes moving between readers possible at all.

There is no IANA registration, so the `x-` form is what tools send and expect. The outline structure itself is generic, and a few outliners and mind-mapping tools use it for its original purpose.
